newsitem.title: USA: InVision bolts higher on FAA award news.
newsitem.headline: InVision bolts higher on FAA award news.

text.p: InVision Technologies Inc shares jumped after winning a large portion of an FAA contract for its bomb detection devices, and analysts expect others in the industry including Magal Security Systems to get smaller pieces of the pie.
"The fact that InVision got the lion's share is not a surprise but the size of the contract is a bit of a surprise," said R. Robert Goldman, an analyst at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
"It's a plus for the industry and a major boost for InVision," he said.

Goldman said the timing of the award was a surprise to those who had expected the announcement to coincide with the release of a final White House recommendation on the detection machines due February 1, 1997. Indeed, InVision's headquarters were closed for the holidays until January 2.

The White House Commission on Aviation Safety and Security, headed by Vice President Al Gore, in a September 9 interim report recommended that the U.S. government buy significant numbers of bomb detectors to install at U.S. airports. The panel was set up after the explosion of TWA Flight 800 off New York July 17, killing all 230 people aboard.

InVision late Thursday won a $52 million Federal Aviation Administration contract for 54 explosive detection systems. The contract calls for the company to deliver the first unit in January and the rest over 12 months. The government has the option to buy more systems in the second year which would boost the contract's value to $110.9 million.

John Westergaard of Westergaard On-line Systems said Congress had appropriated $144 million so far for bomb detection devices. "This contract is a major coup for InVision but I would be very surprised if Magal doesn't get a piece of it also." Magal was unchanged at five in U.S. trading.
"I would also expect some additional dollars to be allocated to other participants," he added.

Josephthal's Goldman agreed, noting that "the Gore commission's initial recommendation thought it should be necessary to include other technologies and other types of bomb detections other than the CAT scans like InVision."

Among others in the group, EG&G Inc rose 1/2 to 20-1/2, Vivid Technologies Inc was unchanged at 10-3/4, American Science & Engineering Inc added 5/8 to 11-3/8, Barringer Technologies Inc rose 1/8 to 7-1/8 and Thermedics Inc slipped 3/8 to 18-5/8.

Goldman said ICTS Holland Productions BV, unchanged at 9-1/8, might be another beneficiary. "Now that a sizeable order has been placed, there's certainly a need for personnel to operate the machines. ICTS has the experience to train and provide the personnel," he said.

Westergaard said, "InVision and Magal really have a leg up on this market place. Their technologies are different but complementary. Magel's system is fast and can screen a lot of bags. I think both will participate."
